identification.summary: TA406 is Proofpoint's designation for a North Korea-aligned actor engaged in credential phishing, intelligence collection, and (per Proofpoint's 2021 report) cryptocurrency-targeting and sextortion activity [S1][S6]. Proofpoint has tracked it since 2018, with campaigns low-volume until January 2021 [S1]. In 2025 Proofpoint reported it shifting to Ukrainian government targets, with activity that others track as Opal Sleet and Konni [S2][S3].
identification.firstObserved: Proofpoint: tracked since 2018; campaigns low-volume until January 2021 [S1].
identification.notes: Proofpoint's 2021 report treats TA406 as one of several actors behind activity publicly tracked as Kimsuky, Thallium and Konni Group [S1]. Secondary summaries of the same report differ on whether Proofpoint ties TA406 to those names, so treat the overlap as unresolved [S1][S5]. The 2025 reporting says other vendors track the activity as Opal Sleet and Konni [S2]. Proofpoint also used TA408 and TA427 for other Kimsuky-linked clusters, so those should not be merged with TA406 [S1]. The imported record lists no MITRE group ID and no Microsoft name; none was confirmed in sources gathered.

attribution.sponsor: North Korea-aligned (Proofpoint's wording). Proofpoint says the targeting serves interests of the North Korean government [S1][S2].
attribution.confidence: Proofpoint describes TA406 as North Korea-aligned and assesses the 2025 Ukraine campaigns as gathering strategic intelligence on the Russia-Ukraine war [S2]. Proofpoint noted that the compromised domain used in earlier credential lures was previously used for Naver credential harvesting, consistent with historical TA406 activity, but did not claim high-confidence attribution of that domain to TA406 [S2]. No government attribution was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Proofpoint email-telemetry and campaign analysis, 2018-2025 [S1][S2]. Primary Proofpoint pages could not be fetched; content is taken from search-result excerpts and secondary coverage [S3][S5].

objectives: Collection of political and strategic intelligence of interest to the North Korean government, and per Proofpoint's 2021 report financially motivated activity including cryptocurrency theft and sextortion [S1][S6]. In 2025 Proofpoint assessed the Ukraine-focused phishing aimed to gauge Ukraine's resolve and the war outlook, and likely to help North Korean leadership assess risk to its forces supporting Russia [S2].

targeting.notes: 2021 campaigns ran almost weekly from January to June against foreign policy experts, journalists and NGOs; a March 2021 campaign reached senior elected officials, defense and law enforcement bodies and financial organizations [S1]. Before 2025 targeting was reported as mainly Russian entities [S2].

capabilities.summary: TA406 usually relies on credential phishing rather than malware; two notable 2021 campaigns delivered information-gathering malware, and Proofpoint names KONNI, BabyShark and QuasarRAT in that report [S1][S5]. In 2025 lures impersonated a fictitious fellow at a non-existent think tank (Royal Institute of Strategic Studies) and linked to password-protected RAR archives on MEGA containing HTML and CHM files with embedded PowerShell that performed system reconnaissance; Proofpoint could not confirm the final payload [S2][S3]. Earlier 2025 emails spoofed Microsoft security alerts sent from ProtonMail, with a compromised domain (jetmf[.]com) used for credential harvesting [S2].

diamond.adversary: North Korea-aligned actor tracked by Proofpoint as TA406, overlapping with Konni / Opal Sleet reporting [S1][S2].
diamond.capability: Credential phishing, spoofed security alerts, MEGA-hosted password-protected archives with HTML/CHM and PowerShell reconnaissance, and in 2021 KONNI, BabyShark and QuasarRAT [S1][S2][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: ProtonMail sending accounts, a compromised domain (jetmf[.]com), and MEGA file hosting [S2].
diamond.victim: Policy experts, journalists, NGOs, government and financial bodies in 2021; Ukrainian government entities in 2025 [S1][S2].
diamond.socioPolitical: North Korean interest in the Russia-Ukraine war outlook and risk to deployed forces; 2021 financial motives [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Email and webmail credential exposure (including Microsoft and Naver lures) and user handling of archives from file-sharing services [S2].

gaps: Proofpoint primary pages (Triple Threat 2021 and TA406 Pivots to the Front 2025) could not be fetched; details come from search excerpts and secondary coverage, so wording and dates should be verified against the originals [S1][S2].
Whether and how TA406 maps to Kimsuky, Thallium, Konni and Opal Sleet is inconsistently described in secondary summaries; Microsoft's own mapping was not checked.
No MITRE ATT&CK group ID, Microsoft actor name, or government attribution was confirmed.
Final payload of the 2025 Ukraine campaign was not identified by Proofpoint [S2].
Scale and success of cryptocurrency theft and sextortion activity are not quantified in sources gathered [S1].
Proofpoint reporting after May 2025 was not found.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Webmail and cloud-identity accounts of policy, diplomatic and defense-adjacent personnel, and file-sharing links reaching government mail, are key terrain. STEP 2: The actor reuses a small set of tactics (credential lures, spoofed security alerts, think-tank personas) and targeting follows North Korean interest in the Russia-Ukraine war [S1][S2]. STEP 3: Template is persona-driven phishing, then credential harvest or archive-delivered scripted reconnaissance. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued phishing of Ukraine, Russia and Western policy communities for strategic intelligence. MDCOA is use of harvested personal or official accounts to reach defense or allied-coalition personnel with tailored lures. Candidate indicators: emails from free providers impersonating think-tank fellows, MEGA links to password-protected RAR files, CHM/HTML files launching PowerShell, and fake Microsoft security alerts [S2].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track vendor reporting on this cluster and its overlaps with Kimsuky/Konni, since naming is inconsistent. (2) Authorities: personal webmail used by service members and policy staff falls outside DoD-managed defenses, so awareness and reporting channels need command emphasis. (3) Mission assurance: protect accounts of staff engaged in Ukraine, Russia and Korea policy. (4) Coordination: share indicators with allied and partner cyber elements through established channels [S1][S2].
